claims.text: A minor addition of an element that forms stable bonds with phosphorus will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
The same minor addition will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The selected baseline alloy tends to crystallize during cooling from the melt under conventional processing conditions.
The intervention is a controlled minor addition of an element having strong chemical affinity for phosphorus.
The intervention should be effective at cooling rates typical of bulk amorphization.
The intervention should stabilize the amorphous state during isothermal holds below the crystallization onset temperature.
The intervention may lose effectiveness when the added-element concentration is too high.
The intervention may lose effectiveness when cooling is so rapid that chemical interactions cannot influence nucleation.
The addition will form stable phosphorus-rich complexes or clusters.
These phosphorus-rich complexes or clusters will impede atomic rearrangements required for crystallization.
Selective bonding between the added element and phosphorus will reduce phosphorus mobility.
Selective bonding and reduced phosphorus mobility will increase the nucleation barrier for crystalline phases.
Enhanced local chemical order will broaden the glass-forming range.
Enhanced local chemical order will delay crystallization during heating.
The modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the otherwise comparable baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization onset temperature than the otherwise comparable baseline alloy.
Excessive addition may promote secondary-phase formation.
The optimal identity and concentration of the alloying addition are uncertain.
